text: A frost flower is a delicate sculpture of ice that grows out of a plant's stem on a very cold morning. It can look like a tiny white rose, a curl of cotton candy or a ribbon of tissue paper. Some are no bigger than a coin. Others stand as tall as a coffee mug.

They form when the air drops below freezing but the soil is still warm enough to stay liquid. The plant's roots keep pulling up water. When that water reaches the frozen stem, it squeezes out through hair-thin cracks and freezes the moment it meets the air. More water pushes the ice outwards, layer by layer. By the time the Sun climbs high, the flower has melted away.

st.prompt: Where does the water in a frost flower come from?

options.t: From inside the plant's stem, pulled up from the still-unfrozen ground
From frozen dew that lands on the stem overnight
From fog that freezes as it blows past

st.reveal: The roots are still drawing water from warm soil. As it reaches the freezing stem, the water squeezes out through tiny cracks and freezes in thin sheets, which are pushed outwards as more water arrives behind them.

d.try: Watch ice grow from below. Fill a plastic tray with damp sand, push a drinking straw in so it stands upright, and put the tray in the freezer overnight. Next morning, look at the top of the straw and the sand around it with a magnifying glass. Draw any needles or crusts of ice you see and notice which way they point.
myth: Frost flowers are just ordinary frost that has settled on a plant.

Ordinary frost grows from water vapour in the air. Frost flowers come from liquid water inside the plant, which is pushed out and freezes in sheets. That is why they curl outwards from the stem instead of coating it.
facts: thin, curling ribbons of ice that grow out of plant stems
the first hard frosts of late autumn, before the ground freezes

sec.t:
Only some plants do it. In the eastern and central USA, the champion is white crownbeard, a tall weed that farmers call frostweed for exactly this reason. Yellow ironweed and a small mint called dittany are also famous for it.

What these plants share is a stem that stays full of water after the leaves have died. The first hard frost splits the outer stem lengthwise. From then on, each cold night can squeeze out a new flower, though the stem gets more battered each time. Most plants manage only a handful before the ground freezes solid and the water supply stops.

sec.h: Hair ice: grown by a fungus
sec.t:
In the forests of Europe, people sometimes find dead branches sprouting what looks like silky white hair. This is hair ice. Each strand is about a hundredth of a millimetre thick, much finer than a human hair, and can be up to 20 cm long.

In 1918, Alfred Wegener, the scientist famous for the idea of [[@continental-drift|drifting continents]], guessed that a fungus was involved. Nearly a hundred years later, in 2015, scientists in Germany and Switzerland proved him right. A fungus living in the wood, called *Exidiopsis effusa*, shapes the ice. Scrape the fungus away, or kill it, and the wood grows only a lumpy crust. Somehow, a living [[fungus|fungus]] sculpts strands of ice finer than cotton thread.

There is a third kind, far from any garden. On calm, freezing nights in the [[@arctic|Arctic]] and Antarctic, new sea ice can sprout fields of frost flowers a few centimetres high. They grow from vapour rising off the thin ice and are about three times saltier than seawater.

Scientists who studied them found the salty petals crowded with bacteria, far more than in the seawater underneath. A fresh field of sea frost flowers can stretch to the horizon, glittering like spilled salt.

Frost flowers are hard to photograph because they barely last. Sunlight or a breath of warm wind turns them back to water within an hour or two. Some nature lovers walk the same patch of woodland every November, hoping for one perfect morning. And even the toughest frost flower is softer than a single grain of [[@snow-hail|hail]], which can fall as hard as a stone.

text: Each kind of fig tree has its own kind of tiny wasp that pollinates it.
Without the wasps, no fig seeds. Without figs, no wasp babies. They need each other.
This partnership is tens of millions of years old. One major study of fig and wasp family trees put it at about 75 million years.

frames.cap: A fig is really a ball of hundreds of tiny flowers growing inside.
A tiny female fig wasp squeezes in through a hole so small it rips off her wings.
Inside, she spreads pollen from her old fig and lays eggs in some flowers.
Her babies grow up inside. The new females fly off carrying pollen to another fig. And so on, for millions of years.

quiz.prompt: A female fig wasp squeezes into a fig to lay her eggs. What happens to her wings on the way in?

options.t: She folds them neatly and flies out later
They are torn off by the tight entrance
She leaves them outside to collect afterwards

quiz.reveal: The entrance to a fig is a tiny hole packed with overlapping scales. Squeezing through tears off her wings and often bits of her antennae. She never leaves. After laying eggs and spreading pollen, she dies inside the fig.

d.try: Look inside a fig. Ask an adult to cut a fresh or dried fig in half. Use a magnifying glass to look at the hundreds of tiny strands and seeds inside. Each one came from a tiny flower. Find the little hole at the bottom of the fig, the only doorway a fig wasp can use.
myth: Every fig you eat is full of dead wasps.

Many figs sold in shops come from varieties that ripen without wasps at all. In wild figs that are pollinated, the wasp that dies inside is broken down by the fig's own enzymes, so there is nothing crunchy left of her.

sec.t:
A fig looks like a fruit, but it starts as something stranger. It is a hollow ball lined on the inside with hundreds of tiny flowers. They never see sunlight and no bee can reach them. The only way in is a narrow hole at the bottom, sealed by tight, overlapping scales.

That hole is the fig wasp's doorway. Each wasp species is built to fit the figs of its own tree species, and in most cases, no other insect can do the job.

A female fig wasp, smaller than a grain of rice, hatches inside a ripe fig. Before she leaves, she collects [[pollen|pollen]] from the fig's male flowers. Then she flies off, following the scent of a tree of her species whose figs are ready.

She forces her way through the scales of a young fig, tearing off her wings. Inside, she lays her eggs in some of the flowers and brushes pollen onto others. The flowers with eggs feed her young as they grow. The flowers with pollen make seeds. Then she dies.

Weeks later, her young hatch. The wingless males hatch first, find the females, mate with them, and chew a tunnel to the outside so the females can escape. The males never leave the fig. The females fly off carrying pollen, and the cycle starts again.

{{story:buddha}}

Figs and their wasps have been evolving together for so long that their family trees match closely. When a new kind of fig appeared, a new kind of wasp often appeared with it. Scientists call this coevolution, when two species shape each other over many generations, a special case of [[evolution|evolution]].

The partnership isn't always perfectly neat. Some figs have two or more wasp species, and some wasps visit more than one kind of fig. There are also cheater wasps that lay eggs in figs without carrying pollen. Even so, it is one of the closest partnerships in nature.

Different fig trees in a forest fruit at different times, so there are almost always ripe figs somewhere. In dry seasons, when other fruit is scarce, figs keep many animals alive. Hornbills, barbets, bulbuls, fruit [[@bats-fly|bats]], monkeys and squirrels all feast on them. That makes figs a lifeline for whole [[@rainforests|forests]], from the Western Ghats to the Amazon.

India has many native figs, including the [[@banyan|banyan]], the peepal and the cluster fig, or *gular*, whose figs grow in bunches straight from the trunk. The peepal is sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. The [[@buddha|Buddha]] is said to have reached enlightenment beneath one at [[@bodh-gaya|Bodh Gaya]].

Fig wasps aren't the only tiny partners plants depend on. [[@chocolate-tree|Cacao]] trees need midges, and many crops need bees. If the fig wasps of one tree species disappeared, that fig could no longer make seeds, and the animals that eat its fruit would feel it too.

text: India's towns and temples are full of monkeys, mostly of two kinds. Macaques, such as the rhesus macaque in the north and the bonnet macaque in the south, are stocky, brown and bold. Langurs are long-limbed and grey, with black faces and very long tails.

Both have learned to live close to people. Monkeys find easy food near homes, markets and temples, and in many places people feed them, partly because monkeys are linked to [[@myths-hanuman|Hanuman]], the monkey god of the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]].
Living side by side isn't always easy. Monkeys can snatch food, bite and raid crops, while people cut down forests and build roads through their homes. Both sides are still working out how to share.

st.prompt: In India's forests, chital deer often feed right under trees full of langurs. Why?

options.t: The langurs groom the deer's fur
The langurs drop food and shout warnings about tigers
The deer just like the shade

st.reveal: Langurs are messy eaters and drop leaves and fruit that the deer gobble up. From high in the trees they also spot tigers and leopards early and give loud alarm calls. The deer, with their sharp noses, can smell danger the langurs can't see. Both sides win.

d.try: Watch a group of pigeons, crows or squirrels from a quiet spot for ten minutes. Write down who eats first, who chases whom and whether one animal seems to keep watch. Scientists who study monkeys start with exactly this kind of patient noting.
myth: Monkeys in the wild eat mostly bananas.
Wild monkeys eat leaves, fruit, flowers, seeds, insects and sometimes eggs. Langurs live mainly on leaves. Most bananas monkeys get come from people.
facts: rhesus macaque, bonnet macaque, grey langur
several chambers, a bit like a cow's
born dark brown, turn grey later

sec.t:
Langurs are leaf-eaters. Leaves are tough and not very nourishing, so langurs have a stomach with several chambers, a bit like a cow's. Helpful bacteria inside break down the leaves. Langur mothers often let other females in the group hold and carry their babies, which are born dark brown and slowly turn grey.

Macaques eat almost anything: fruit, seeds, insects, flowers and food from bins. They have stretchy pouches inside their cheeks, so they can grab food quickly and chew it later somewhere safe. This is one reason they do so well in cities. Clever and quick, they have been known to unzip bags and open fridges.

In Delhi, thousands of rhesus macaques live around government buildings, parks and homes. For years, officials hired handlers with trained langurs to scare them off, because macaques fear langurs. When keeping langurs this way was stopped under wildlife law, some men were hired to imitate langur calls instead.

In [[@india-wonder-hill-stations|hill towns]] like Shimla, macaques snatch food and glasses from tourists. Experts say feeding monkeys makes things worse. Monkeys that rely on handouts lose their fear of people, form bigger groups and grow more aggressive when the food stops. In some places, scientists are trying birth control to slowly bring numbers down.

The rhesus macaque has played a large part in science. In 1949, a rhesus monkey called Albert II flew to space on a US [[@rockets-how|rocket]], years before any human did.

In 1940, scientists studying the blood of rhesus monkeys discovered a substance that most people also carry. They named it the Rh factor, after the monkey. It is the plus or minus in [[@blood-groups|blood groups]] like A+ or O−.

There are even rhesus macaques in the USA. In the 1930s, a tour boat operator released a few on an island in a Florida river to entertain visitors. Nobody told him monkeys can swim. Their descendants now number in the hundreds and roam the forests nearby.

Not all Indian monkeys are thriving. The [[@wild-lion-tailed-macaque|lion-tailed macaque]], with its silver mane, lives only in the [[@rainforests|rainforests]] of the Western Ghats and is endangered. The golden langur, with fur like polished brass, lives in a small area of western Assam and Bhutan.

These monkeys need forest, not city streets. Their future depends on keeping the trees standing.

text: The bombardier beetle keeps two chemicals in a sac at the tip of its abdomen. They are hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, the same hydrogen peroxide used in some first-aid kits. On their own, they don't do much.

When an ant, frog or bird attacks, the beetle squeezes some of this mix into a second, armoured chamber full of enzymes. The enzymes set off a violent reaction. In an instant, the liquid heats up to around 100 °C, the boiling point of water, and blasts out of the beetle's rear with a pop. The spray is hot, smelly and stinging, and most attackers quickly let go.

st.prompt: How does the bombardier beetle stop its own body from being cooked by its boiling spray?

options.t: It keeps the chemicals apart until the moment it fires, mixing them in a tough chamber
Its body is made of metal
It cools the spray with ice inside its body

st.reveal: The beetle stores its two main chemicals in one sac and the enzymes in a separate, hard-walled chamber. Only when it fires does it squeeze them together. The reaction happens in that chamber and shoots straight out of the tip of its abdomen.

d.try: Fill a clean squeeze bottle with water. Try squirting it at a target in one long stream, then in many quick, short squeezes. Which goes farther and which is easier to aim? Bombardier beetles fire in rapid pulses rather than one long blast.
myth: The bombardier beetle's spray is so hot it could badly burn a person.

The spray is hot and stings, and it can stain skin brown, but the amount is tiny. It is a powerful weapon for ants, frogs and toads, not a serious danger to people. It is still best not to pick one up.

hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, mixed with enzymes

sec.t:
The beetle's weapon works like a tiny engine. In one species, scientists found it doesn't fire one big blast but about 500 small ones every second. Each little explosion pushes open a valve, lets out a puff of spray, and then the valve closes again, ready for the next.

That pulsing helps protect the beetle. Firing in short bursts gives the chamber walls a moment to cool between pops. In 2015, researchers used powerful X-ray cameras to watch the reaction happen inside living beetles.

The beetle can aim, too. Some can swivel the tip of the abdomen and spray forward, sideways or even over their own backs. Thomas Eisner, a famous American insect scientist, spent years filming beetles to show how well they aim.

The heat comes from the reaction. When the enzymes break down hydrogen peroxide, they release oxygen and lots of heat. The hydroquinones turn into benzoquinones, irritating chemicals that sting and smell. The fast release of gas pushes it all out.

Engineers have studied the beetle to design better fuel injectors and fire extinguishers, because it sprays an exact amount at high speed without blowing itself up. Some rocket fuels also use hydrogen peroxide, which is broken down quickly to make hot gas, a cousin of [[@rocket-fuel|rocket fuel]] chemistry.

There are hundreds of kinds of bombardier beetles, and they live on every continent except Antarctica. In India, some are brightly marked in yellow and black, a warning colour that tells predators to stay away. They usually hide under stones and leaves by day and hunt small insects at night.

Many hunters, from spiders to birds, have learned to leave them alone. Frogs and toads still try, which keeps the experiments going. The beetle's trick makes it one of the best defended small [[@insects-importance|insects]] in the world.

The bombardier beetle has long been a favourite example in debates about evolution, because its system seems so complex. Biologists have shown that simpler versions exist in related beetles, each step useful on its own, so a hot spray could have built up gradually. Its watery cousin in the sea, the [[@power-pistol-shrimp|pistol shrimp]], also uses heat as a weapon, in a bubble that flashes for less than a blink.

text: Things slow down because of friction. When one surface slides or rolls over another, the two rub and grip. Friction is the force that resists that movement, and it always pushes against the direction something is moving.

Even surfaces that feel smooth are rough when seen very close up. Under a microscope, polished steel looks like a range of tiny hills and valleys. When two surfaces touch, those bumps catch on each other, and at the points where they press hard together, atoms on each side stick a little. Breaking those contacts takes effort. That effort becomes heat, which is why your hands warm up when you rub them together.
Air causes friction too. It's called air resistance, or drag, and it's why a dropped feather drifts while a stone plunges.

st.prompt: You slide an ice cube and a wooden block of the same size across a smooth kitchen floor with the same push. What happens?

options.t: The wooden block goes further, because it's harder
The ice cube goes further, because it has less friction
They stop at the same place

st.reveal: Ice is slippery because its surface is coated with a very thin, watery layer, which lets it slide easily. The wooden block's rough surface grips the floor and slows it down much faster.

d.try: Shuffle two thin notebooks together, page over page, so the pages overlap by a few centimetres. Now hold each spine and try to pull them apart. Then try again with only five pages overlapping. Friction between many pages adds up to a surprisingly strong grip.
myth: Moving things slow down and stop naturally, because motion just runs out.

Moving things keep going unless a force acts on them. Here on Earth, friction and air resistance are almost always acting, so things stop. In space, with almost nothing to rub against, a spacecraft can coast for decades.
facts: a force that resists things sliding or rolling over each other
tiny bumps and sticky contact between surfaces

sec.t: Leonardo da Vinci, the painter of the *Mona Lisa*, filled notebooks with drawings of blocks being dragged across tables. Around 1500, he worked out that the friction on a block depends on how hard it presses down, not on how big its bottom surface is. His notes stayed unpublished for centuries. The French scientist Guillaume Amontons found the same rules again in 1699, and today they are often named after him.

It's easy to think of friction as the enemy. Without it, though, you couldn't walk. Your shoes would skid on the floor as if it were oiled ice. Knots would slip undone, nails would slide out of wood, and [[@pencils|a pencil]] would leave no mark on paper.

[[@tyres|Car tyres]] and [[@shoes-history|running shoes]] have patterned treads to grip the road. Brakes work by pressing pads against a spinning disc or wheel, turning the car's motion into heat. Cricket fast bowlers shine one side of the ball on their trousers. A smooth side and a rough side drag the air differently, which helps the ball [[@cricket-swing|swing]].

When we want things to move freely, we fight friction. Oil and grease fill in the tiny bumps so surfaces slide past each other. Ball bearings, small steel balls inside a wheel's hub, let parts roll instead of scrape. The [[@wheel-invented|wheel]] itself is the oldest friction-beater of all: rolling a load is far easier than dragging it.

Ice skaters glide because ice has a very thin, slippery layer on top. Scientists are still arguing about exactly what makes that layer, but it lets a skater cross the rink with a single push. A bobsled run goes further, smoothing and icing the whole track so sleds can reach well over 100 km/h.

text: A printer turns a picture on a computer into marks on paper. Most home and office printers are one of two kinds.

An inkjet printer squirts tiny drops of liquid ink onto the paper through rows of very fine nozzles. A print head slides back and forth across the page as the paper moves forward, building the picture line by line.

A laser printer works more like a photocopier. A laser draws the page onto a drum using [[@static-electricity|static electricity]]. A dry powder called toner sticks to the charged parts, rolls onto the paper and is melted in place by heat.
Both build each page out of tiny dots. Look closely at any printout and you can see them.

st.prompt: A colour printer has cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink. How does it print green?

options.t: It puts tiny dots of cyan and yellow close together
It keeps a secret green cartridge
It mixes the inks in a little cup first

st.reveal: The dots are so small that your eye blends them. Cyan and yellow dots side by side or on top of each other look green. By changing how many dots of each colour it uses, the printer can make thousands of shades.

d.try: Look at a printed photo in a newspaper or magazine through a magnifying glass. You'll see that the picture is made of tiny dots of a few colours. Try making your own dot picture with felt-tip pens using only blue, pink and yellow dots, and step back to see what colours appear.
myth: When a printer says its ink is empty, the cartridge has run completely dry.
Many printers warn early to protect the print head, so some ink is often left in the cartridge. Some keep printing for a while after the warning.
facts: each a few trillionths of a litre

sec.t:
Many inkjet printers use heat. Behind each nozzle is a tiny heater. When an electric pulse heats it for a few millionths of a second, a little of the ink boils into a bubble. The bubble pushes a drop out of the nozzle and onto the paper. Then the bubble collapses, and fresh ink flows in.

This happens thousands of times a second in each of hundreds of nozzles. Each drop is tiny, a few trillionths of a litre, far smaller than a speck of dust you could see. Canon called its version Bubble Jet. HP's ThinkJet went on sale in 1984.

Other inkjet printers use a crystal that bends when electricity passes through it. The crystal squeezes the ink like your fingers squeezing a toothpaste tube.

In 1969 an engineer at Xerox named Gary Starkweather had an idea. A photocopier already used light to make a pattern of static charge on a drum. What if a laser drew the pattern instead, straight from a computer?

He built one, and by 1971 it was working at Xerox's research lab in California. Laser printers became common in offices in the 1980s.

Inside, the laser beam bounces off a spinning mirror and sweeps across a charged drum, line by line. Where the light hits, the charge changes. Toner, which is fine plastic powder mixed with colour, sticks only to the right places. A hot roller then melts it into the paper. That is why pages come out of a laser printer warm.

{{story:printing-press}}

Colour printers usually have just four inks: cyan (a bright blue), magenta (a pinkish purple), yellow and black. Printers call this CMYK, with K standing for black.

By laying tiny dots of these colours side by side or on top of each other, the printer can fool your eye into seeing almost any colour. Cyan and yellow make green. Magenta and yellow make red. All three together make a muddy dark brown, which is why printers add real black for crisp text.

This is different from a screen, which mixes red, green and blue light. That is why a photo can look a little different on paper than it did on your phone.

The idea of building a picture from dots, one line at a time, is used far beyond offices. Printers make T-shirt designs, labels, wallpaper and big posters for buses. Special printers press dots into paper so blind readers can feel [[@braille|Braille]].

[[@3d-printing|3D printers]] take the idea a step further. Instead of one layer of ink, they lay down layer after layer of melted plastic, building up a solid object from the bottom.

Some scientists have even used inkjet-style printers to place living cells in neat patterns. The printer on a home desk, built to print homework, shares its idea with some of the most advanced machines in medicine.

text: Zardozi is a kind of heavy embroidery made with metal thread. The name comes from Persian: zar means gold and dozi means embroidery. Artisans stitch shining wire, sequins, beads and tiny coiled springs onto silk or velvet to make raised patterns that glitter like jewellery.

It was a favourite of the [[@mughals|Mughal]] emperors, who wore it on robes, turbans and slippers, and used it on tents, cushions and the saddles of their horses. Today zardozi is used most on wedding clothes: lehengas, sherwanis, dupattas and bridal bags. Lucknow, Bareilly, Agra, Varanasi and Bhopal are among its biggest centres.

st.prompt: In most zardozi made today, what is the shiny metal wire usually made of?

options.t: Copper or silver wire coated with a thin layer of gold or gold colour
Solid pure gold
Shiny plastic

st.reveal: Old royal zardozi often used real gold and silver. Today, to keep costs down, most work uses copper or silver wire with a thin gold or gold-coloured coating. It still shines, but costs far less.

d.try: Draw a simple flower or paisley shape on a piece of cardboard. Glue on bits of shiny foil, sequins or old bindis along the outline, then fill the inside with small loops of golden wool or string. Hold it under a lamp and tilt it to see how raised shapes catch the light.
myth: Zardozi is the same as zari.

They are related but different. Zari is the metallic thread itself, often woven into fabric like the borders of Banarasi saris. Zardozi is heavy embroidery stitched on top of cloth with that thread plus sequins, beads and coiled wire.

sec.t:
Metal can't be pulled through cloth like cotton thread. So zardozi workers use metal in clever shapes. Gold or silver is drawn through smaller and smaller holes until it becomes a wire finer than a hair. Some of it is wound around a silk core to make a thread called kasab.

Other wire is coiled tightly into hollow springs called salma and dabka. Workers cut these into tiny pieces and stitch them down like beads. Add little metal discs called sitara (stars) and glass beads, and a flat cloth becomes a raised, shining surface. Gold is so soft that a single gram can be drawn into a wire more than two kilometres long. Because metal work is heavy and scratchy, zardozi is usually stitched onto strong fabrics like velvet, satin or thick silk that can bear the weight.

Gold embroidery is old in India. Ancient texts describe garments worked with gold. But zardozi reached its peak in the 1500s and 1600s, when emperors like [[@akbar|Akbar]] ran royal workshops full of craftspeople. Robes, canopies and even elephant coverings were covered in gold and silver.

When royal money dried up in the 1700s, many artisans lost their patrons. Some moved to the courts of nawabs and other rulers, including Lucknow and Hyderabad. The craft survived, but it became smaller and quieter for a long time.

Lucknow is famous for two embroideries. One is delicate white [[@art-chikankari|chikankari]], stitched in white thread on light cotton. The other is glittering zardozi. In 2013, Lucknow zardozi received a GI tag, a legal label linking the craft to the region around the city.

Tens of thousands of families in and around Lucknow, Bareilly and nearby towns work in zardozi, many from home. Much of the work is done by men, though more women now work too.

Most zardozi now goes into Indian [[@weddings-india|weddings]], where a gold-heavy outfit is a family tradition. It also turns up on film costumes and fashion runways in Paris and New York. Some military badges and crests worn on uniforms around the world are stitched with the same kind of metal thread work.

And the strangest part? All the [[@gold-where|gold]] ever mined, more than 200,000 tonnes by 2024, would fit in a cube about 22 metres on each side. Every gold thread in a royal robe was a sliver of something very rare.

text: Humans are social animals. For most of our history, people lived in small groups where everyone depended on each other for food, safety and care. Friends helped you survive, so our brains evolved to want company and to feel uneasy when we are alone too long.

Today, friends still matter for our health and [[@happiness|happiness]]. They help us share good news, get through hard times, try new things and laugh. Research suggests that people with close relationships tend to be healthier and live longer. [[@loneliness|Long-term loneliness]], on the other hand, has been linked to health problems.

sec.t:
In 1938, researchers at Harvard University began following a group of young men, and later added their families. The Harvard Study of Adult Development has checked on them for more than 80 years, through jobs, marriages, wars and old age.

Its present director, psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, says the clearest finding is that people with warm, close relationships were happier and healthier as they aged. Good relationships predicted long, healthy lives better than wealth, fame or social class.

In 2023, the US Surgeon General, America's top public health official, issued a warning about loneliness. The report said long-term loneliness can raise the risk of [[@heart-health|heart disease]], stroke and [[@mental-health|depression]]. It compared the health risk of serious social isolation to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day, a figure drawn from a large review of earlier studies.

Feeling lonely sometimes is normal, especially after moving to a new school or city. If loneliness lasts a long time or feels heavy, talking to a parent, teacher or counsellor can help.

Friendships take time. In one study, researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes about 50 hours together to go from strangers to casual friends, and more than 200 hours to become close friends. Shared activities help: playing on the same team, working on a project, or simply sitting together at lunch every day.

British anthropologist Robin Dunbar argued that most people can keep up roughly 150 meaningful relationships, with only about five in the innermost circle. Other scientists dispute the exact number, but most agree that close friends are few.

Friendships are not always easy. Friends argue, drift apart or change as they grow. Psychologists say the friendships that last usually involve trust, listening, keeping promises and saying sorry after a mistake. [[@kindness-science|Kindness]] helps both sides.

Online friendships can be real and important too, though experts suggest balancing screen time with time spent together in person. A friend who laughs at your jokes, sits with you when you are sad and [[@truth-lies|tells you the truth]] when you need it is worth more than a long list of contacts.

text: A loan is money you borrow now and pay back later. The money you borrow is called the principal. On top of it, you usually pay [[interest|interest]], a kind of rent for using someone else's money. Interest is usually given as a percentage per year.

If you borrow ₹1,00,000 at 10% a year, you pay ₹10,000 a year in interest on top of returning the original amount. Families borrow to buy homes, students to pay for college, farmers to buy seeds, and businesses to grow. Loans make big things possible sooner, but they cost extra, and they must be paid back.

st.prompt: You borrow ₹10,000 at 10% interest a year, compounded yearly. If you pay nothing back, roughly how much will you owe after 7 years?

options.t: About ₹19,500, nearly double
Exactly ₹17,000
About ₹11,000

st.reveal: Simple interest would add ₹1,000 a year, making ₹17,000. But compound interest charges interest on the interest too. After 7 years at 10%, the debt is about ₹19,487. The Rule of 72 predicts doubling in about 72 ÷ 10 = 7.2 years.

myth: Interest is a fee that only borrowers pay.

Interest works both ways. When you put money in a savings account, the bank borrows it and pays you interest. The bank then lends money to others at a higher rate, and the difference helps pay its costs.

sec.t:
Someone who lends money gives up the chance to use it themselves. There is also a risk that the borrower won't pay it back. And prices usually rise over time, because of [[@inflation|inflation]], so money paid back later buys a little less. Interest makes up for all three.

That is how a [[@money-banks|bank]] works. You keep savings in the bank, and the bank pays you interest, say 3% to 7% a year. The bank lends that money to others at a higher rate, perhaps 8% to 11% for a home loan in India. The difference pays for staff, buildings and losses on loans that go bad, and leaves some profit.

With simple interest, you pay interest only on the original amount. Borrow ₹1,00,000 at 10% for three years and you pay ₹10,000 each year, ₹30,000 in total.

With [[@maths-money-compound|compound interest]], unpaid interest is added to the debt, and next year you pay interest on that too. After year one you owe ₹1,10,000. After year two, ₹1,21,000. After year three, ₹1,33,100. It grows faster each year, like a snowball rolling downhill. This is the same doubling pattern described by [[@exponents|exponents]].

A handy shortcut called the Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double. Divide 72 by the interest rate. At 8% a year, savings double in about 9 years. At 36% a year, which some credit cards charge on unpaid bills, a debt doubles in about 2 years.

{{story:money-banks}}

Most home and car loans in India are repaid through EMIs, or equated monthly instalments. Each month you pay the same amount. Early on, most of it is interest. Later, more of it pays off the principal. A 20-year home loan can end up costing well over the price of the house once all the interest is added.

Credit cards are short-term loans. If you pay the full bill on time, there is usually no interest. If you don't, the interest rate is often very high, frequently above 30% a year in India, and around 20% or more in the United States.

Lending is ancient. The Code of Hammurabi, carved in Babylon around 1750 BCE, set the highest interest a lender could charge on grain and on silver. Many religions have also had rules about charging interest.

In [[@villages-india|Indian villages]], farmers have often borrowed from local moneylenders at very high rates, sometimes losing their land when they could not repay. The writer [[@premchand|Premchand]] described this hardship in his novel *Godaan*. In [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], Muhammad Yunus started Grameen Bank, which gave very small loans to poor villagers, mostly women, who could not get bank loans. He and the bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

text: A googol is the number 1 followed by 100 zeros. Mathematicians write it as 10¹⁰⁰.

The name was invented by a child. Around 1920, the American mathematician Edward Kasner asked his nine-year-old nephew, Milton Sirotta, to think up a name for a very large number. Milton suggested "googol". Kasner liked it and used it in his lectures, and in 1940 he put it in a popular book, *Mathematics and the Imagination*.

Milton also suggested an even bigger number, a "googolplex". He said it should be one followed by as many zeros as you could write before getting tired. Kasner made it more exact: 1 followed by a googol zeros.

st.prompt: Is a googol bigger or smaller than the number of atoms in the whole observable universe?

options.t: Much smaller
About the same

st.reveal: Scientists estimate there are about 10 to the power of 80 atoms in the observable universe, a 1 with 80 zeros. A googol has 100 zeros, so it's about 100 billion billion times bigger. There isn't enough stuff in the universe to count to a googol with.

myth: The word "googol" came from the company Google.

It's the other way round. "Googol" was invented around 1920 and printed in a maths book in 1940. Google's founders picked their name in the 1990s, and the usual story is that it came from a misspelling of googol.

sec.t:
A googol is far bigger than anything you could count. Scientists estimate that the observable universe contains about 10⁸⁰ atoms. A googol is 10²⁰, or a hundred billion billion, times bigger than that.

A googolplex is unimaginably bigger again. Even writing it out is impossible. There aren't enough atoms in the universe to make the zeros, even if each atom were a single zero.

Kasner wanted children to see that a number can be huge without being [[@infinity|infinite]]. A googol is enormous, but you could still add one to it.

sec.t:
In India, big numbers have their own names. A lakh is 1,00,000 and a crore is 1,00,00,000. Indian commas are placed differently too, after every two digits once you pass a thousand, so that lakhs and crores are easy to read.

The names keep going. A hundred crore is an *arab*, and a hundred arab is a *kharab*. Ancient texts in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] list number names much further. The Yajurveda names powers of ten up to *parardha*, a million million. A Buddhist text called the *Lalitavistara* tells how the young Siddhartha, later [[@buddha|the Buddha]], named numbers in a contest, climbing to one with 53 zeros.

The word "million" comes from Italian and means roughly "a big thousand". "Billion" was created later. But for centuries, countries disagreed about what a billion meant.

In the United States, a billion has always meant a thousand million, 1,000,000,000. In Britain, it used to mean a million million. In 1974, the British government began using the American meaning, and today most English-speaking countries do the same. Some European languages still use the older meaning, which can cause mix-ups in [[@translation|translation]].

Number words often hide old ideas. "Eleven" and "twelve" come from Old English words meaning "one left over" and "two left over", counting past ten on your fingers. In [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], many numbers between 20 and 100 have names that are quite irregular, which is one reason children take time to learn them.

Different [[@languages-world|languages]] count in different ways. In French, 80 is *quatre-vingts*, "four twenties", a leftover from counting in twenties. Every one of these words is a small piece of history.

text: An impossible shape is a drawing that looks like a solid 3D object but could never exist in real life. Each small part of it makes sense. Put the parts together, though, and they contradict each other.

The most famous is the Penrose triangle. It seems to be made of three square beams joined at right angles. Follow the beams around and you end up where you started, which can't happen with three right angles in real space. Our brains are built to read flat pictures as solid objects, and they check one corner at a time. That is why the trick works so well.

st.prompt: Artists have built real sculptures that look like a Penrose triangle. How do they do it?

options.t: The beams don't really join, and the trick only works from one angle
They bend space with magnets
They use very flexible metal

st.reveal: The real object is an open shape, with one corner far closer to you than the others. From one exact viewpoint, the gap hides behind the beam in front, and your brain fills in a closed triangle.

myth: Impossible shapes are just bad drawings with mistakes in them.

Each corner of an impossible shape is drawn correctly. The trick is that the corners can't all be true together. Our brains check small parts of a picture at a time, so we don't notice the whole thing breaks the rules of space.
facts: first drawn by Oscar Reutersvärd in 1934, made famous by Lionel and Roger Penrose in 1958
a staircase that seems to go up forever in a loop

sec.h: The triangle with three right angles
sec.t:
In a normal triangle on paper, the three corners add up to 180 degrees. In the Penrose triangle, each corner looks like 90 degrees, adding up to 270. Only on a curved surface like a globe can a triangle's angles go above 180, and the Penrose triangle is drawn as straight beams in flat space.

The Swedish artist Oscar Reutersvärd drew the first version in 1934, made of cubes. In 1958, the British scientist Lionel Penrose and his son Roger, later a Nobel Prize winner in physics, published it as an "impossible object". They also invented the endless Penrose stairs.

The Dutch artist M. C. Escher loved these ideas. In 1960 he drew *Ascending and Descending*, in which monks march round the endless stairs on a rooftop. In 1961 came *Waterfall*. Water flows down a channel, along a zigzag and somehow ends up higher than it started, then pours over a wheel and back to the start. It looks like a machine that runs forever.

Escher returned to strange geometry again and again, from lizards that tile a page to ants marching round a [[@puzzle-mobius|Möbius strip]]. His [[@maths-art-escher|maths art]] still turns up in maths classrooms all over the world.

Another favourite is the devil's fork, or blivet. At one end, it has three round prongs. At the other, they become two square bars. Look at either end on its own and it's fine. Look at the whole thing and your eyes keep sliding back and forth, trying to make it fit.

It spread widely in the 1960s, when it appeared on magazine covers as a puzzle for readers.

Your eyes receive a flat image, like a photo. Your brain turns it into a 3D world using clues: lines that meet at corners, shading, and things in front hiding things behind. This is the same skill that lets artists use [[@perspective|perspective]] to make paintings look deep.

These shortcuts are usually right, so the brain trusts them. Impossible shapes break the rules in a way that each shortcut alone can't catch.

Some artists build real objects that look impossible from one spot. In Perth, Australia, a giant aluminium impossible triangle stands in a park. From the right angle it looks closed. Walk a few steps and it falls apart into three beams.

The Japanese mathematician Kokichi Sugihara makes small models where balls seem to roll uphill towards a peak. They won prizes in the Best Illusion of the Year contest. Seen from another side, the "uphill" slopes actually point down. These are all [[@optical-illusions|optical illusions]], proof that seeing isn't always believing.

text: A mascot gives an event a friendly face. A sports tournament, a festival or a company is a big, hard-to-picture thing. A cheerful cartoon animal is easy to remember, draw and love, especially for children.

Mascots also do practical jobs. They appear on posters, tickets, badges and toys, and selling those toys helps pay for the event. They often show off something from the host place, like a local animal or symbol. Inside the stadium, a person in a big costume dances, waves and keeps the crowd happy during the boring bits. That's a lot of work for one smiling character.

The word did start with lucky charms, but there's no evidence that mascots change results. What they can do is lift the mood of a crowd and give fans, especially children, something to cheer for.

sec.t:
The word comes from the French mascotte, meaning a lucky charm. It spread after a French comic opera called La Mascotte became a hit in 1880. The story's heroine brings luck to whoever keeps her close.

At first, a mascot could be any lucky object or animal. Soldiers kept goats and dogs as regimental mascots. Sports teams in the United States started keeping live animals, like bulldogs and goats, at their games. Over time, many teams switched to costumed characters, which don't get scared by a roaring crowd.

India's most loved mascot is probably Appu, the baby elephant of the 1982 [[@asian-games|Asian Games]] in Delhi. He was a cheerful cartoon elephant, and he was everywhere: on posters, badges and Doordarshan. Two years later, Delhi opened an amusement park called Appu Ghar, named after him.

For the 2010 [[@commonwealth-games|Commonwealth Games]], also in Delhi, the mascot was Shera, a cartoon tiger. Tigers are India's national animal, and the design was meant to say that India was strong and ready.

Companies use mascots too, and some are older than any sports mascot. The Michelin Man, made of tyres, dates from 1898. In India, the little Amul girl in her polka-dot frock has appeared on [[@amul|Amul]] butter adverts since 1966. Her billboards make jokes about the week's news, and people look out for them.

These characters work because people trust faces. Studies of [[@advertising|advertising]] show that children recognise brand characters from a very young age. That's one reason some countries have rules about using cartoon mascots to sell sugary food to children.

Being a costumed mascot is harder than it looks. The suits are heavy and hot, and in an Indian summer or a Texas afternoon the person inside can overheat quickly. Many performers can see only through a small mesh panel, so a helper often walks beside them. Most mascots also have a rule never to speak, because a real voice would break the spell for young fans.

Mascots sometimes have to change. In the United States, many school and sports teams once used names and mascots based on Native American people. Many Native groups said these were hurtful stereotypes. Over the years, many teams changed them, including two big professional teams in 2020 to 2022.

Even small details matter. Designers now test mascots with children before launch, to check that they look friendly and not scary. Somewhere, a design team is already arguing about what the mascot for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics should look like.

text: An Indian fighting kite, or *patang*, is made from a square of very thin paper stretched over two strips of split bamboo. One strip, the *dhaddha*, runs straight down the middle. The other, the *kamaan*, is bent into a bow across the top. Paper is glued around them, and a small triangle of paper is often added at the bottom.

What makes it a fighting kite is the string. Flyers use *manja*, cotton thread coated with a paste of glue and powdered glass. When two kites cross in the sky, their strings rub, and the sharper or more cleverly handled one cuts the other free. The cut kite drifts away, and children on rooftops and in lanes run to catch it.

st.reveal: Fighting string is coated with a gritty paste. When two strings cross, flyers either pull in fast or let out string fast. The rubbing works like sandpaper, and the weaker string snaps first.

sec.t:
Most children's kites have tails to keep them steady. A patang doesn't. That makes it unstable: it twists and dips with every gust. A beginner finds it frustrating. An expert loves it.

By tugging and loosening the string, a skilled flyer can make the patang turn, dive and climb in a second. That control is what wins a fight. The light bamboo frame flexes just enough, and the [[@bamboo|bamboo]] itself is strong for its weight. Bamboo is a grass, and some kinds can grow nearly a metre in a single day.

The biggest kite day in India is Makar Sankranti, called Uttarayan in Gujarat, around 14 January. In [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]], families spend the day on their terraces with food, music and stacks of patangs. When someone cuts a rival's kite, they shout "Kai po che!", meaning roughly "I've cut it!" Gujarat has hosted an International Kite Festival since 1989, with flyers from dozens of countries.

Kites also fill skies on Independence Day in Delhi, on Basant Panchami in Punjab and during Sankranti in Hyderabad and Jaipur. Each region has its own words and its own favourite kite shapes.

sec.h: The dark side of the string
sec.t:
Manja is sharp enough to cut skin. Every kite season, hospitals treat people with cuts, and there have been serious accidents when loose strings stretched across roads where people rode two-wheelers. Thousands of birds, including pigeons, kites and even [[@vultures-india|vultures]], get tangled every year.

In 2017, India's National Green Tribunal banned nylon and other synthetic manja, often called Chinese manja, because it doesn't break and can't rot. Bird hospitals in Ahmedabad run special rescue camps every Uttarayan. Many families now fly with plain cotton thread instead.

Kites probably began in China more than 2,000 years ago, and travelled along trade routes to India. Mughal paintings show people flying kites, and kite fighting was a favourite sport in the courts of Lucknow. Today, plastic kites are cheaper, but paper and bamboo patangs are still made by hand in small workshops. Each one is light enough to rest on a fingertip, and each one, given a good breeze, can climb hundreds of metres. How it stays up there at all is the story of [[@kite-flying|lift and air pressure]].

text: The appendix is a thin pouch, about the length of your little finger, attached to the beginning of your large intestine on the lower right side of your belly. For a long time, scientists thought it did nothing at all.

Today, many researchers think it has small but real jobs. It is packed with immune tissue, which helps the body learn about the microbes in the gut. Some scientists also suggest it acts as a safe store of helpful [[@digestion-gut|gut bacteria]], ready to repopulate the intestine after an illness clears them out. Still, people who have their appendix removed live normal, healthy lives.

Seeds very rarely have anything to do with it. Appendicitis usually starts when the opening of the appendix gets blocked, often by a small lump of hardened stool or swollen tissue, and then becomes infected.

sec.t:
In 2007, researchers at Duke University in the USA suggested a new idea. The appendix is narrow and tucked out of the main flow of food. If a bad stomach infection, like cholera, washes most bacteria out of the gut, the appendix might keep a store of helpful ones safe. Afterwards, they could spread out again and refill the intestine.

Supporters point to studies showing that the appendix holds a thick layer of bacteria. Other scientists say the evidence is still thin. The debate continues.

Another clue comes from comparing animals. A 2013 study found that an appendix has appeared separately in different groups of mammals at least 30 times, and has rarely disappeared once it evolved. Something that keeps evolving again and again may well be useful.

Appendicitis happens when the appendix becomes blocked, swollen and infected. It is most common in children and young adults. The usual signs are pain that starts near the [[@gross-belly-button|belly button]] and moves to the lower right side, along with fever, sickness or not wanting to eat.

If someone has strong belly pain like this, it is important to tell a parent or trusted adult straight away, so they can get medical help. An infected appendix can burst, which is dangerous. In [[@hospitals|hospitals]] today, doctors usually remove it with a short operation, often through a few tiny cuts. In some mild cases, they treat it with antibiotics instead.

In 1735, a surgeon in London named Claudius Amyand removed an inflamed appendix from an 11-year-old boy. It is often described as the first recorded successful appendix operation. For the next century and a half, though, appendicitis was poorly understood and often fatal.

In 1886, an American doctor, Reginald Fitz, described appendicitis clearly and gave it its name. He urged doctors to operate early. Thanks to good hospitals, anaesthesia and antibiotics, it is now usually a quick fix, and most patients go home within a few days.

text: On Earth, [[gravity|gravity]] pulls on your body every second of your life. Your muscles, bones and heart are built to work against it. In [[@spacecraft-move|orbit]], astronauts are in constant free fall, so they float, and the body behaves as if gravity has almost vanished.

The body quickly starts to change. Fluids drift up towards the head. Muscles and bones get weaker because they [[@what-if-no-bones|aren't needed to hold the body up]]. The spine stretches, eyesight can change, and the sense of balance gets confused.
Most of these changes reverse after astronauts return to Earth, but some take months, and a few may last.

options.t: They are falling around Earth all the time, along with the station
There is no gravity that high up

st.reveal: At the space station's height, gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground. The station and everyone inside it are falling towards Earth, but they are also moving sideways so fast that they keep missing it. Falling together, they float.

d.try: Measure your height against a wall first thing in the morning, then again just before bed, using a book flat on your head and a pencil mark. Most people are about a centimetre shorter at night, because the discs in the spine get squashed during the day. In space, that squashing stops.
myth: There's no gravity in space, which is why astronauts float.
Gravity reaches far into space. It keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth. Astronauts float because they are in free fall, moving around Earth so fast that they keep falling without hitting the ground.

sec.t:
On Earth, gravity keeps much of your blood and other body fluids in your legs. In space, those fluids spread upwards. Astronauts' faces look round and puffy, their noses feel blocked, and their legs get thinner. Astronauts jokingly call this "puffy face, bird legs".

The blocked nose dulls their [[@space-weird-smell|sense of smell]], which also makes food taste bland. Many astronauts start asking for spicy sauces they wouldn't normally want.

The extra fluid around the head can also press on the back of the eyes. Some astronauts on long missions have found their eyesight changes, and NASA studies this closely.

Inside your ear is a balance organ that senses movement and gravity, a bit like a spirit level. In space, it sends confusing signals that don't match what the eyes see. In their first few days, many astronauts feel [[@motion-sickness|space sick]], with headaches and nausea.

The brain adapts within days. But back on Earth, it has to readjust. Astronauts often walk unsteadily at first, and some say that, after landing, they let go of a cup in mid-air, expecting it to float.

sec.h: Twins and an Indian yogi in orbit
sec.t:
In 2015 and 2016, NASA astronaut Scott Kelly spent 340 days on the space station. His identical [[@twins|twin]] brother Mark, also an astronaut, stayed on Earth. Scientists compared them before, during and after. They found many changes in Scott's body, from his [[@digestion-gut|gut bacteria]] to how his genes were switched on. Most went back to normal within months.

India has its own space story. In 1984, Rakesh Sharma flew to the Soviet Salyut 7 space station. Among his experiments, he tested whether yoga exercises could help the body cope with weightlessness. In 2025, Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian to visit the International Space Station. India's [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] programme aims to launch Indian astronauts on an Indian rocket.

sec.h: Radiation and the road to Mars
sec.t:
Earth's thick air and magnetic field shield us from most radiation from the Sun and deep space. Astronauts above the air get much more, which raises their risk of illness later in life. On the space station, they are still partly protected by Earth's magnetic field.

A trip to Mars could take two to three years there and back. Doctors and engineers are still working out how to keep astronauts' bones, muscles, eyes and minds healthy for that long, far from any hospital.

text: The internet grew out of a small American network called ARPANET, which linked four university computers in 1969. Over the next 20 years, engineers worked out common rules, called protocols, so that different networks could connect into one giant "network of networks".

Email arrived in the early 1970s. The rules that still run the internet, called TCP/IP, were adopted in 1983. In 1989 a British scientist invented the World Wide Web, which made the internet easy for anyone to use. The public could [[@internet-india|get online in India]] from 1995. Today billions of people use it every day.

options.t: Just the letters LO
The word HELLO
A picture of a cat

st.reveal: Charley Kline at UCLA tried to type LOGIN to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, about 500 kilometres away. The receiving computer crashed after L and O. An hour or so later they tried again and it worked.

d.try: Write a short sentence, one word per slip of paper, and number each slip. Hand the slips to different friends, who pass them around the room by different routes before giving them to a "receiver". The receiver puts them back in order using the numbers. This is packet switching, the way the internet breaks every message into small numbered pieces.
myth: The internet was built so the US military could survive a nuclear war.

Some early research on networks, by Paul Baran in the US, did aim to keep communication working after an attack. But the ARPANET itself was built mainly so researchers at different universities could share expensive computers.

sec.t:
Old telephone networks kept a line open for each call. Engineers Paul Baran in the US and Donald Davies in Britain, working separately, came up with a different idea. Chop each message into small blocks, called packets, and send them separately by whatever route is free. At the other end, put them back together.

This is called packet switching, and it is still how the internet works. If one route is blocked, packets simply go another way. When you watch a video, it arrives in thousands of packets that may travel by different paths.

On 29 October 1969, a student named Charley Kline at the University of California, [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]], tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute. He typed L, then O, then the system crashed. So the first message on the network was "LO". Within weeks, four computers were linked.

In 1971, programmer Ray Tomlinson sent the first network [[@email|email]] between two computers. He chose the @ sign to separate a person's name from their computer's name, because it was rarely used for anything else.

By the 1970s, other networks were springing up, including ones using radio and [[@satellites-help|satellites]]. They could not talk to each other. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed a shared set of rules, TCP/IP, describing how packets should be addressed and checked. On 1 January 1983, ARPANET switched over. Many people call that the true birthday of the internet.

Most of the internet's data now travels as flashes of light through glass fibres. [[@undersea-internet|Cables run along the ocean floor]] between continents, some as thick as a garden hose. They carry far more data than satellites do.

The internet was still hard to use until 1989, when Tim Berners-Lee, working at the CERN laboratory near Geneva, invented the [[@web-invented|World Wide Web]]. The internet is the network of connections. The web is the pages and links that run on top of it.

India's public internet service was launched by VSNL, the state telephone company, on 15 August 1995, Independence Day. Connections were slow dial-up lines and costly. Today India has hundreds of millions of internet users, most of them on mobile phones. To see how your messages find their way today, read [[@internet-how|how the internet works]].

text: Patent offices have approved some very strange ideas. There's a patent for exercising a cat with a laser pointer, one for swinging on a swing and one for a comb-over hairstyle. There was even one for the wheel itself, renamed a "circular transportation facilitation device".

A patent is a legal right that lets an inventor stop others copying their invention, usually for about 20 years. To get one, an idea must be new, not obvious to experts, and described clearly. It doesn't have to be a good idea. That's why the record books are full of odd ones, and why some were later cancelled.

options.t: To show that a new fast patent system didn't check ideas properly
Because he thought nobody had invented it yet
To charge car makers money

st.reveal: Australia had just started a quick "innovation patent" that was granted without a full check. John Keogh applied for the wheel, under a fancy name, to prove the point. It worked, and the case won him a joke prize, an Ig Nobel.

Patent offices check whether an idea is new and not obvious, and whether it could work. They don't judge whether it's sensible, so some very silly ideas have been granted. Others, like the wheel, slipped through by mistake and were later cancelled.

sec.t:
In 2001, Australia started a fast-track "innovation patent". It was granted quickly, without a full check by an examiner. A patent lawyer named John Keogh thought this was a bad idea. To prove it, he applied for the [[@wheel-invented|wheel]], describing it in fancy legal language.

It was granted. The story spread around the world, and later that year Keogh and the patent office shared an Ig Nobel Prize, a joke award for research that "makes people laugh, then think". The patent was later cancelled. Australia eventually scrapped innovation patents altogether.

sec.h: The cat, the swing and the comb-over
sec.t:
In 1995, two Americans received a US patent for a "method of exercising a cat". It describes shining a laser pointer on the floor so a cat chases the dot. Plenty of cat owners had done it for years.

In 2002, a five-year-old named Steven Olson got a patent for a "method of swinging on a swing", by pulling sideways on the chains. His father, a patent lawyer, wanted to teach him about patents. The patent office later re-examined it and cancelled it. More young inventors appear in the story of [[@inventions-kids|kid inventors]].

In 1977, a father and son from Florida patented a method of combing hair to cover a bald spot. It also earned an Ig Nobel Prize, in 2004.

Not every strange patent is useless. Many inventions seemed silly at first: Velcro, the microwave oven and the first aeroplanes all drew laughs. But badly checked patents can cause trouble. Companies sometimes collect patents on obvious ideas and threaten to sue others, which is why patent offices try hard to reject them.

India's patent office has its own rules. Indian law doesn't allow patents on things like traditional knowledge already known for centuries. In the 1990s, a US patent on using turmeric to heal wounds was challenged by India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, which showed that the idea appeared in old Indian texts. The patent was cancelled in 1997.

Odd patents remind us that inventing is part creativity and part paperwork. Many brilliant inventions never got patents, and many patents never became anything. And the laser in that cat-exercising patent is itself one of the great inventions, a story told in [[@lasers|how lasers work]].

text: A maglev train floats because powerful [[@magnets-how|magnets]] push or pull it up off its track, with a gap of somewhere between about 1 and 10 centimetres. The word maglev is short for magnetic levitation. Levitation just means rising into the air without support.

With nothing rolling on a rail, there is no wheel [[@friction|friction]] and very little shaking. The train is pushed forwards by more magnets. Electricity running through coils in the track creates a magnetic wave that travels along the line. The train is pulled with it, a bit like a surfer riding a wave. Speed up the wave, and the train speeds up too.

st.prompt: Once a maglev train is floating, what slows it down the most at high speed?

options.t: The air it has to push out of the way
Rubbing against the rails
The weight of the passengers

st.reveal: A floating train doesn't rub on its track, so the biggest drag at high speed is air. That's why maglevs have long, pointed noses, and why pushing through air takes much more power as speed rises.

src: Central Japan Railway Company (JR Central), the SCMaglev and Chuo Shinkansen.

myth: Because maglev trains don't touch the track, nothing slows them down once they are moving.
There's no rolling friction on the rails, but air still pushes back hard. At 400 km/h, air resistance is the main thing the train fights, so it needs plenty of power to keep going.

sec.t:
The world's best-known working maglev links Shanghai's Pudong airport with the edge of the city, a line of about 30 km. It opened for regular passengers in 2004, using German technology. For years it ran at up to 431 km/h in daily service. Since 2021 it has been held to 300 km/h, which still makes the trip in about eight minutes. A digital sign inside the train shows the speed climbing. Outside, cars on the highway seem to go backwards.

It's a thrilling ride, but it has not been copied widely. The line cost a great deal, it only goes a short distance, and passengers still have to change to the metro to reach the city centre.

Japan already runs some of the world's best [[@bullet-trains|bullet trains]] on ordinary steel wheels. Even so, it is building a maglev line, called the Chuo Shinkansen, between [[@tokyo|Tokyo]] and Nagoya. Much of it runs in [[@tunnels|tunnels]], including under the Japanese Alps.

On its test track, a seven-car maglev reached 603 km/h in 2015, a world record for trains. The finished line should make the Tokyo to Nagoya trip in about 40 minutes, less than half today's time. Construction has been delayed, and it is not expected to open before the 2030s.

Maglev trains can't use ordinary railway tracks. Every kilometre of guideway must be built from scratch, very precisely, and that is expensive. Ordinary high-speed trains, which reach about 300 to 350 km/h, can share existing stations and tracks, and are good enough for most journeys.

Still, the idea keeps returning. China has tested new maglev trains designed for 600 km/h, and engineers in India have studied it too. Supporters point out that maglevs are quiet, smooth and need fewer repairs, because no wheels grind against rails. Critics answer that the money could build many more kilometres of ordinary fast railway. For now, if you want to float across the countryside, Shanghai is the place to go.

text: Africa is the second-largest continent, and over thousands of years it was home to many powerful kingdoms. Egypt is the most famous, but it was far from alone.

To Egypt's south lay Kush, whose kings once ruled Egypt itself. In the highlands of Ethiopia stood Aksum, a great trading power. In West Africa, the empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai grew rich on gold. In the south, people built the stone city of [[@great-zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]]. Each had its own rulers, beliefs, art and trade links reaching across oceans and deserts.

st.reveal: Salt was scarce in the forests and grasslands of West Africa, and people needed it to stay healthy and to preserve food. Camel caravans carried slabs of rock salt from the Sahara and traded them for gold.

Africa had powerful kingdoms, rich trading cities, universities, libraries and stone monuments for thousands of years. Some colonial writers claimed outsiders must have built places like Great Zimbabwe, but archaeologists proved that Africans built them.

sec.t:
Kush grew up along [[@egypt-nile|the Nile]] in what is now Sudan. For centuries [[@ancient-egypt|Egypt]] ruled it. Then, in the 700s BCE, Kushite kings marched north and ruled Egypt as pharaohs for about a century.

Later, the Kushites built their capital at Meroë. They buried their kings and queens under small, steep pyramids. Sudan has more than 200 of them, more than Egypt. Meroë was also a centre of ironworking, with heaps of slag, the waste left from smelting iron, still visible today.

In West Africa, the Ghana Empire (not the same place as modern Ghana) controlled trade routes across the [[@sahara|Sahara]]. Camel caravans carried [[@salt|salt]] south and gold north. Arab writers called Ghana "the land of gold".

The Mali Empire followed. In 1324 its ruler, [[@mali-empire|Mansa Musa]], made the pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge caravan. He handed out so much gold in [[@world-cairo|Cairo]] that, according to the writer al-Umari, its value there stayed low for years afterwards. Mali's city of Timbuktu became famous for its scholars and libraries, and families there still keep thousands of old manuscripts.

The traveller [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] visited Mali in the 1350s. He wrote that its roads were safe and its people strict about justice.

In southern Africa, between about 1100 and 1450, the ancestors of the Shona people built Great Zimbabwe. Its biggest structure, the Great Enclosure, has a curving granite wall about 250 metres long and up to 11 metres high, made of stones fitted together without mortar. The city was a hub of trade, and archaeologists have found glass beads from India and pottery from China there.

In the forests of what is now southern [[@nigeria|Nigeria]], the Kingdom of Benin made thousands of brass and bronze plaques and heads. Artists worked in a guild that served the king. Their plaques once covered the wooden pillars of the royal palace, showing kings, warriors, ceremonies and even Portuguese traders who arrived by sea in the late 1400s. Benin City itself was ringed by long earthen walls and ditches, dug by hand over centuries. In 1897 British soldiers looted the royal city and carried many to Europe. Today museums are debating how many should go home, and some, including pieces from Germany, have already been returned to Nigeria.

text: Crown jewels are the crowns, sceptres, orbs, swords and other precious objects used by kings and queens, especially at coronations, when a new monarch is crowned. They are meant to show power, wealth and history, and each object has a meaning. An orb stands for the world, a sceptre for the power to rule.

Many countries have, or once had, crown jewels. Britain's are the most famous, kept in the Tower of London and seen by millions of visitors. Iran, Denmark, Sweden and others also keep royal treasures. In India, the jewels of the Nizams of Hyderabad and the treasures of other princely states tell a similar story of royal splendour.

st.reveal: After King Charles I was executed in 1649, Parliament ordered the royal regalia to be destroyed. Gold was melted into coins and gems were sold. When the monarchy returned in 1660, new crowns had to be made.

sec.t:
Britain's crown jewels include about 100 objects set with more than 23,000 gems. The heaviest crown, St Edward's Crown, weighs about 2.2 kg, as much as two big bags of sugar. It is used only at the moment of crowning, because it is so heavy.

The Sovereign's Sceptre holds Cullinan I, about 530 carats, one of the largest cut diamonds in the world. It was cut from the Cullinan diamond, found in South Africa in 1905, which weighed about 3,106 carats, roughly the size of a fist. The Imperial State Crown includes nearly 3,000 diamonds.

The crown made for Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother, holds the [[@kohinoor|Kohinoor]], taken from Punjab in 1849.

In 1671, Thomas Blood, an Irish adventurer, tried to steal the jewels. Dressed as a clergyman, he befriended the elderly keeper of the jewels, then attacked him. Blood flattened the crown with a mallet to hide it under his cloak, while his friends grabbed the orb and sceptre.

He was caught near the Tower gate. Oddly, King Charles II pardoned him and even gave him land. Nobody knows exactly why. Since then, the jewels have been guarded far more closely, behind thick glass and steel in the [[@london-tower|Tower of London]].

India's princely states had dazzling collections. The Nizams of Hyderabad were among the richest rulers in the world. Their jewels included the Jacob Diamond, about 184 carats, which the last Nizam reportedly found in his father's slipper and used as a paperweight.

In 1995, the Government of India bought 173 pieces of the Nizams' jewellery. They are kept in the vaults of the Reserve Bank of India and shown at the National Museum in New Delhi only occasionally. The Mughal emperors also had legendary treasures, including the Peacock Throne, which was carried off to Persia in 1739.

On 19 October 2025, thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris. In less than eight minutes, they stole eight pieces of jewellery linked to French queens and empresses, valued at about 100 million US dollars. They also dropped a crown that belonged to Empress Eugénie, which was found broken outside. Several suspects were arrested, but by mid-2026 the stolen jewels themselves had not been found.

Crown jewels are made to last forever, but history keeps proving how fragile they are. Wars, revolutions and thieves have broken up many collections. Some of those [[@treasure-hunts|lost treasures]] are still being hunted today.

text: In 1848 gold was found in the hills of northern California. When the news spread, people poured in from the eastern United States, Latin America, Europe, China and Australia, all hoping to get rich quickly.

They were called forty-niners, after 1849, the year the rush really took off. California changed almost overnight. It became a US state in 1850, and [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] grew from a small settlement into a busy port city. But the rush was a disaster for the Native peoples who already lived there.

st.reveal: Gold is soft. Fool's gold, a shiny mineral called pyrite, shatters when struck, but real gold flattens like dough. They also boiled a flake in strong soap made with lye, and it stayed bright.

Most found little or nothing and many went home poorer. The easy surface gold was gone within a few years, and big companies with machines took over.

sec.t:
James Marshall was building a sawmill for a landowner named John Sutter at Coloma, in the Sierra Nevada foothills. On 24 January 1848 he saw shiny flakes in the water channel below the mill. After a few simple tests, the workers were sure it was gold.

Sutter tried to keep it secret, but it was hopeless. A shopkeeper in San Francisco ran through the streets holding up a bottle of gold dust. Soon sailors left their ships in the bay to go digging, and the town nearly emptied.

By 1850 hundreds of abandoned ships crowded San Francisco's harbour. Some were dragged ashore and turned into shops, hotels and even a jail. As the town filled in the shoreline, many hulls were buried, and builders digging foundations downtown still sometimes find their timbers today.

At first, gold lay in riverbeds where anyone could find it. Miners scooped up gravel in a pan and swirled it with water. Gold is heavy, about 19 times heavier than water, so it sank while the sand washed away.

Soon that easy gold ran out. Miners built long wooden boxes called sluices, and later companies blasted hillsides with powerful jets of water. This hydraulic mining washed huge amounts of mud into rivers and damaged farmland so badly that a court largely banned it in 1884.

Most miners found little. Prices in mining towns were sky-high, so a pair of boots or a dozen eggs could cost a day's earnings. Shopkeepers, hotel owners and traders often did better than diggers.

One of them was Levi Strauss, a young German immigrant who sold cloth and goods in San Francisco. Years later, in 1873, he and a tailor named Jacob Davis patented work trousers strengthened with metal rivets, the ancestors of today's [[@jeans|jeans]].

Before the rush, about 150,000 Native people lived in California. Miners took their land and food sources, brought new diseases, and attacked villages, often with little or no punishment. By around 1870, only about 30,000 Native Californians remained. Historians now see this as one of the darkest chapters of [[@native-nations|Native American]] history.

India has gold-mining history too. At the Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka, miners dug for over a century until 2001, reaching more than 3 km underground, among the deepest mines in the world.

text: The Hoysalas ruled southern [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] from about the 11th to the 14th century. Their kings and nobles paid for more than a hundred temples. The best known, at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, are famous for carving so dense that hardly a patch of wall is left plain.

Two things made this possible. The sculptors worked in a grey-green soapstone, called chloritic schist, which is soft and fine-grained when freshly cut, so it could be carved almost like wood. And Hoysala patrons wanted their temples to dazzle, competing to hire the most skilled artists. Many sculptors signed their work, which tells us they were proud of it.

They were carved by hand with chisels, hammers and files about 800 years ago. The soapstone the sculptors used is soft when freshly quarried, which made very fine work possible.

sec.h: A king, a tiger and a name
sec.t:
Hoysala legend tells of a young man named Sala who was learning at a temple when a tiger attacked. His teacher shouted, "Hoy, Sala!", meaning "Strike, Sala!", and Sala killed the tiger. The story gave the family its name, and a figure fighting a tiger became the royal emblem.

The Hoysalas began as hill chiefs in the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]]. By the early 1100s, under King Vishnuvardhana, they had become a major power. Their capitals were first Belur and then Dorasamudra, today's Halebidu, whose name means "old capital".

sec.h: Belur: a temple for a victory

sec.t:
The Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu, begun around 1121, is a pair of shrines joined together. Its walls carry thousands of figures, including gods, dancers, musicians and animals, and scenes from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]].

Inside, the pillars are round and ringed, as if made on a giant lathe. Historians think the stone was turned while workers held cutting tools against it, though exactly how is still discussed. The surfaces are so smooth that they reflect light like polished metal.

Many Hoysala temples stand on a raised platform, called a *jagati*, wide enough for worshippers to walk around the shrine. Seen from above, many of these platforms are shaped like stars.

The star plan multiplied the corners of the building. Every corner made another wall for carving and threw a different shadow as the sun moved. The Keshava temple at Somanathapura, completed in 1268, has three star-shaped shrines on one platform. In 2023, Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura were named [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Sites]] together as the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas.

In 1311 an army of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]], led by Malik Kafur, attacked Dorasamudra. The Hoysalas survived, but grew weaker. The last major king, Veera Ballala III, died in battle in 1343. Out of the turmoil, new rulers founded the [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] Empire, which carried south Indian art forward. The Hoysala temples, many still in use, kept their stone dancers frozen mid-step.

text: Bengaluru, the capital of Karnataka, did not become a tech city by accident. In the 1900s it gathered science institutes, aircraft factories and India's space agency. These trained thousands of engineers. When computer companies began looking for skilled people in the 1980s, Bengaluru was ready.
Its cool climate, colleges and English-speaking workers helped too. Today the city is home to thousands of software firms and start-ups, and to well over a crore people.

It is right beside the ocean

st.reveal: Air gets cooler as you go higher. Bengaluru sits about 920 m up on the Deccan Plateau, so its days are warm rather than scorching. That pleasant weather drew British officers, retired people and, later, companies and students.
