myth: Bangalore got its name from a story about boiled beans.

A popular tale says a hungry king was given boiled beans (benda kaalu) by an old woman. But an inscription from around 890 CE, found near the city, already mentions a place called Bengaluru, so the name is older than the story.

sec.h: A mud fort and a garden
sec.t:
In 1537, a chieftain named Kempe Gowda I built a mud fort and laid out markets around it. Later rulers Hyder Ali and his son [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]] started Lalbagh, a huge garden, in the 1760s. The British built a large army base here in 1809, which brought roads, churches and schools.

Lalbagh's glasshouse, built in 1889, still hosts flower shows. Under the garden lies a low hill of ancient rock about 3,000 million years old. The Geological Survey of India has declared it a National Geological Monument. With its parks and tree-lined roads, Bengaluru became known as the Garden City.

In 1909 the Indian Institute of Science opened, set up with money from the industrialist Jamsetji Tata. C. V. Raman worked here, and it trained generations of scientists. In 1940 an [[@made-planes|aircraft factory]] was founded, which became Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. After independence, defence and electronics companies settled in the city.

The Indian Space Research Organisation, [[@isro-launch|ISRO]], has its headquarters in Bengaluru. [[@satellites-help|Satellites]] are built here, and the teams that guide [[@isro-missions|ISRO's missions]] to the Moon and Mars work from the city.

Software needs people more than factories. A company setting up in the 1990s needed thousands of engineers, cheap office space and reliable links to customers abroad. Bengaluru had engineering colleges all around it, a mild climate that made long days easier, and a reputation as a science city. When one big company arrived, others followed, and so did the engineers. Economists call this clustering: firms gather where the skilled workers are, and workers move to where the jobs are.

So much growth so quickly has brought problems. Traffic jams are famous, and a short drive can take an hour at rush time. Bengaluru once had hundreds of lakes, many dug centuries ago as tanks to store rainwater. Many have been built over or polluted. Bellandur Lake was in the news for clouds of toxic foam. Citizens' groups and the city are now working to clean up the [[@wetlands|lakes and wetlands]] that remain.

Kannada is the state's language, but people in Bengaluru speak Tamil, Telugu, Hindi, Malayalam, English and many more. Engineers from across India and abroad have made it one of India's most mixed cities, much like its neighbour [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]]. In 2014 its name officially changed from Bangalore back to Bengaluru, the name Kannada speakers had always used.

text: Chilika is a huge shallow [[lagoon|lagoon]] on the coast of Odisha. It is separated from the Bay of Bengal by a long, thin strip of sand, but a narrow mouth lets the sea flow in and out. Rivers pour fresh water in from the land side. The result is brackish water, partly fresh and partly salty.

It is the largest coastal lagoon in India, covering about 900 square kilometres in the dry season and more than 1,100 in the monsoon. Its waters hold dolphins, fish, crabs and prawns, and in winter it becomes one of the biggest bird gatherings in Asia.

st.prompt: Chilika is joined to the sea by a narrow mouth. What happened when that mouth slowly filled with sand in the 1990s?

options.t: Less sea water came in, and fish catches fell
The lake turned into a desert

st.reveal: With less sea water flowing in, the lake became less salty, weeds spread and fish and prawns that need salty water declined. In 2000 a new mouth was dug, sea water returned, and the catch rose again.

myth: Chilika is a freshwater lake like any other.
Chilika is a lagoon. Rivers bring in fresh water from the land and tides bring in salt water from the sea, so its water is brackish, and it is saltier near the sea mouth than in the north.

sec.t:
Because Chilika mixes river and sea, its water is not the same everywhere. Near the sea mouth it is quite salty. In the north, where rivers like the Daya flow in, it is almost fresh, especially after the monsoon.

That variety makes room for a lot of life. Scientists have recorded hundreds of kinds of fish, prawns and crabs in the lagoon. Many of them grow up in Chilika and swim out to sea as adults. The shallow water, rarely more than a few metres deep, warms quickly in the sun and grows plenty of tiny plants and animals for young fish to eat. Seagrass meadows on the lake floor give them places to hide. Around 2 lakh people in fishing villages around the shore depend on the lake for their living, some using methods passed down for generations, like the families described in [[@fishing-boats|India's fishing communities]].

Chilika is home to Irrawaddy dolphins, grey, round-headed dolphins with no beak that live in coasts, lagoons and rivers in South and Southeast Asia. Their population worldwide is small, and Chilika holds one of the most important groups. In the 2025 census, 159 were counted in the lake.

Boats from Satapada, near the sea mouth, take tourists to watch them. Too many noisy motorboats can disturb the dolphins, so local rules try to limit how close boats go. Fishing nets are another danger, because a dolphin caught underwater can drown.

In the 1980s and 1990s, Chilika began to choke. Mud from deforested hills upstream filled the lake, and the sea mouth kept silting up. Less sea water came in, weeds spread, and fish catches fell sharply. In 1993 the lagoon was put on the Montreux Record, a list of [[@wetlands|wetlands]] in danger kept under the Ramsar Convention.

In 2000, the Chilika Development Authority dug a new mouth to the sea. Salt water flowed back in, weeds shrank and fish, prawns and dolphins recovered. In 2002, Chilika became the first Asian site removed from the Montreux Record.

Chilika has several islands. On one stands the Kalijai temple, which pilgrims reach by boat, especially during the festival of Makar Sankranti. Another, Honeymoon Island, is popular with visitors for its clear water. In the early morning, fishers' boats spread across the lake, and the line between water and sky can be hard to see.

text: The Forbidden City is a vast palace in the middle of Beijing, the capital of China. It was the home of China's emperors and the centre of their government from 1420 until 1912. It was called "forbidden" because nobody could enter or leave without the emperor's permission.

It covers about 72 hectares, about 100 football fields, and is surrounded by a 10-metre wall and a wide moat. Inside are around 90 courtyards and about 8,700 rooms, with golden-yellow roofs and red walls. Since 1925 it has been a museum, called the Palace Museum, and it is one of the most visited places on Earth.

st.reveal: Golden yellow was reserved for the emperor in imperial China. Almost every roof is yellow-tiled. The walls are painted red, a colour linked with good luck and happiness.

That is a popular legend, linked to the idea that only heaven could have 10,000 rooms. A careful count in the 1970s found about 8,700 rooms.

sec.t:
In 1402, a prince seized the throne of the Ming dynasty and became the Yongle Emperor. He decided to move the capital north from Nanjing to Beijing, and ordered a new palace. Work began in 1406.

Huge numbers of workers took part, often said to be around a million, including some 100,000 skilled craftsmen. Giant logs of rare nanmu wood were dragged from forests in the south-west. Massive stone slabs were slid along roads that workers flooded with water in winter, so it froze into ice tracks. The palace was finished in 1420.

The emperor lived with his family, hundreds of servants, officials and guards. In the inner court, where the imperial family lived, the only grown men allowed apart from the emperor were usually palace servants called eunuchs. At some times, thousands of them worked in the palace.

Few outsiders ever saw the emperor. Officials who did had to kneel and touch their heads to the ground. Those who broke the palace's rules could be severely punished.

In 1644, the Ming dynasty fell, and the Manchu rulers of the Qing dynasty took over the palace. In total, 24 emperors lived there over nearly 500 years.

In 1912, after the [[@chinese-revolution|revolution]] that made China a republic, the last emperor, a six-year-old boy named Puyi, gave up the throne. He was allowed to keep living in the inner palace until 1924, when he was forced to leave. A year later, the palace opened to the public as a museum.

The Palace Museum holds more than 1.8 million objects, including paintings, porcelain, clocks, jade and bronze. During the 1930s, when Japan invaded China, staff packed many treasures into crates and moved them away from Beijing. Some never came back. Part of the collection is now in the National Palace Museum in Taipei, Taiwan.

The Forbidden City now limits how many people can visit each day, and you must book a ticket ahead with your ID. Crowds are biggest during China's national holidays in early October, when lines of visitors stretch across the courtyards. It is closed on most Mondays for cleaning and repairs. With the [[@great-wall|Great Wall]], it is one of the top sights in [[@beijing|Beijing]] for visitors from around the world.

text: Istanbul sits on both sides of the Bosphorus, a narrow strip of sea that joins the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. Geographers draw the line between Europe and Asia along this strait, so the city spills across two [[@continents|continents]]. The old centre, with its palaces and great domed mosques, is on the European side. Millions of people live on the Asian side and cross every day by ferry, bridge or tunnel.

The city grew there for a reason. Whoever held this spot could control ships going between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and roads going between Europe and Asia. For over 1,500 years, that made it the capital of mighty empires.

st.reveal: Istanbul was the capital of the Ottoman Empire for nearly 500 years. When the Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923, its leaders chose Ankara, in the middle of the country, as the new capital.

sec.t:
Greek settlers founded a town called Byzantion here around 660 BCE. In 330 CE, the Roman emperor Constantine made it his new capital and called it Constantinople. After the western half of the Roman Empire fell, the eastern half carried on from here for another thousand years. Historians call it the [[@byzantium|Byzantine Empire]].

In 1453, the young Ottoman sultan Mehmed II besieged the city. A huge chain blocked the harbour, called the Golden Horn. So Mehmed's men built a road of greased logs and hauled dozens of ships over a hill behind the city and into the water beyond the chain. Within weeks the city fell. It became the capital of the [[@ottomans|Ottoman Empire]], and the name Istanbul slowly took over.

sec.h: The church that became a mosque

sec.t:
The Grand Bazaar, opened in the 1460s, is one of the oldest covered markets in the world. Around 4,000 shops line its maze of roofed streets, selling carpets, lamps, spices and gold. Goods from the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] and the spice routes once passed through traders here.

[[@oddity-tulip-mania|Tulips]] grew wild in Central Asia, and Ottoman sultans loved them. They planted tulips in palace gardens and painted them on tiles. In the 1500s tulip bulbs travelled from Istanbul to Europe and on to the Netherlands, where they later became a national symbol.

Istanbul is also famous for its street cats. Thousands roam freely, and shopkeepers and neighbours leave out food and water. Some cats have become local celebrities.

For most of history, the only way across the Bosphorus was by boat. The first bridge opened in 1973. In 2013, a railway [[@tunnels|tunnel]] called Marmaray opened deep under the strait, built in sections on land, then sunk into a trench on the seabed. Digging it up turned out to be a bonus: workers found an old harbour with the remains of dozens of Byzantine [[@shipwrecks|shipwrecks]].

At its narrowest, the Bosphorus is only about 700 metres wide, about the length of seven football fields. Huge oil tankers squeeze through it past the waterfront houses.

text: *Matilda* is a children's novel by the British writer Roald Dahl, published in 1988 with drawings by Quentin Blake. It tells the story of Matilda Wormwood, a brilliant little girl whose parents ignore her, and who finds friendship and safety through books and a kind teacher, Miss Honey.

Readers love it because it is on the side of children. Matilda is small, clever and treated unfairly by grown-ups who should know better. She fights back with brains, pranks and, eventually, a magic power. The villains, her rude parents and the terrifying headmistress Miss Trunchbull, are so over the top that they are as funny as they are frightening.

st.reveal: When Matilda gets very angry at Miss Trunchbull, she finds she can tip over a glass just by staring at it. Later she practises and uses the power to help her kind teacher, Miss Honey.

myth: Matilda is set in the USA.
The book takes place in an English village. The 1996 film moved the story to America, which is why many people remember it that way. The 2022 musical film went back to England.

sec.t:
Matilda's parents prefer television and dodgy car deals. When she asks for a book, her father tells her to watch TV instead. So, at the age of four, she walks alone to the village [[@libraries|library]].

The librarian, Mrs Phelps, helps her choose. After the children's shelves, Matilda moves on to grown-up books, starting with *Great Expectations* by [[@charles-dickens|Charles Dickens]]. Her list includes *Jane Eyre*, *Oliver Twist*, *Animal Farm* and *Kim* by Rudyard Kipling, one of many [[@kipling-india|British writers who wrote about India]].

Books give Matilda a world much bigger than her house. As Dahl puts it, they carry her across the world while she sits in her little room.

{{story:broadway}}

At school, Matilda meets Miss Honey, a gentle teacher who sees how clever she is, and Miss Agatha Trunchbull, the headmistress. The Trunchbull is a former hammer-throwing champion who hates children. She locks pupils in the Chokey, a tall, narrow cupboard lined with spikes. When a boy named Bruce Bogtrotter is caught eating her cake, she forces him to eat an entire giant chocolate cake in front of the whole school, and he triumphantly finishes it. In one famous scene she swings a girl round by her pigtails and throws her over a fence.

Dahl's stories often have cruel adults and brave children. Some readers find them too nasty. But many children love seeing bullies face consequences. In *Matilda*, the meek and the clever win, and the bullies end up running away.

Dahl's first version of Matilda was very different. In the early draft, she was a wicked child who played tricks on her parents just to be mean. Dahl's editor and Dahl himself felt the story wasn't working, and he [[@how-to-write-story|rewrote it almost completely]]. The new Matilda is good-hearted and loves reading. Her pranks, like putting superglue in her father's hat, only come after he has been unfair to her.

Dahl himself was a complicated figure. He wrote much-loved books, but he also made antisemitic remarks during his life. In 2020, his family publicly apologised for them.

In 1996, the actor Danny DeVito directed a film of *Matilda*, set in the USA. In 2010, the Royal Shakespeare Company opened a musical version, with songs by the Australian comedian and composer Tim Minchin. It moved to London's West End and then to [[@broadway|Broadway]] in New York, winning many awards.

In 2022, a film of the musical brought the story back to England. Its songs, like "Revolting Children" and "When I Grow Up", became favourites in school assemblies. The story's message has stayed simple: even if you are small, you can stand up for what is right.

text: Modern writers retell old myths by bringing the gods, monsters and heroes into new settings, often into today's world. They keep the old stories' bones and change the clothes.

In Rick Riordan's *Percy Jackson* books, the Greek gods are alive and living in America. Percy, a 12-year-old in New York, finds out that his father is Poseidon, god of the sea. He goes to a summer camp for children of gods, battles monsters from [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]] and travels across the USA on quests.
Retelling myths is not new. People have done it for thousands of years. What modern writers add is humour, modern problems and heroes young readers can recognise.

st.reveal: Greek myths changed from place to place and writer to writer. Homer, Hesiod, the playwrights of Athens and later the Roman poet Ovid all told stories in their own ways. Retelling myths with new twists is as old as the myths themselves.

myth: Each old myth has one true, fixed version.
Myths were told and retold for centuries, and often exist in many versions. The Ramayana alone has hundreds of retellings across Asia. Modern authors like Riordan are joining a very old tradition.

sec.h: Gods with phones and bad tempers
sec.t:
Riordan's gods are funny, vain and sometimes terrible parents, just like in the old stories. Mount Olympus floats above the Empire State Building in [[@new-york|New York]]. The underworld's entrance is in Los Angeles.

But the monsters and myths are real, taken from ancient sources. Medusa still turns people to stone, though she runs a garden-gnome shop. Readers learn who the Minotaur, the Fates and the Titans were while laughing.

Riordan went on to write series based on Roman, Egyptian and Norse myths, and books retelling Greek myths in Percy's own voice. The first books were made into films in 2010 and 2013. Riordan was unhappy with them, and he worked closely on a later TV series that began in 2023 and stayed nearer to the books.

Myths have always been retold. In [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], poets such as Homer and Hesiod, and later the playwrights of Athens, told the same stories in different ways. The Roman poet Ovid retold hundreds of Greek myths in his *Metamorphoses*, around 8 CE, and changed many of them.

In India, the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and Mahabharata have been retold in nearly every Indian language, in songs, dances, plays, TV serials and films. [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] turned them into comics. Writers like Devdutt Pattanaik retell them for modern readers, and the 1980s TV *Ramayan* drew huge audiences across India.

In 2018, Riordan started a publishing imprint, Rick Riordan Presents, for authors from different cultures to retell their own myths. The first book was *Aru Shah and the End of Time* by Roshani Chokshi. In it, a 12-year-old Indian-American girl in Atlanta accidentally frees an ancient demon. Then she discovers she is the reincarnation of one of the Pandava brothers from the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]]. Another series, by Sayantani DasGupta, draws on Bengali folk tales.

Other authors have retold Norse, [[@myths-maya|Mayan]], Korean and [[@myths-african|West African myths]] for young readers. Each new version changes the old story a little. That is exactly how myths have survived so long: by being told again, to new listeners, in new ways.
